## Overview

peridial is a standardised R framework for ingesting, validating, and summarising clinical peritoneal dialysis (PD) unit data. Four nested S3 classes represent the PD unit, the cohort of patients in the unit, their catheters, and each catheter's peritonitis episodes (if any), supporting reproducible calculation of the International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis (ISPD)-recommended PD unit's peritonitis rate and peritonitis-free percentage indicators from longitudinal PD and PD-related infection records.

This is the vignette to start with. It walks through installation and setup, the example data, building a `pd_unit` from PD unit input files, and the `print()`, `summary()`, `plot()` and `subset()` methods for inspecting what was built.

Two further vignettes go deeper. Both assume you have built a unit as below, and either can be read next:

- `vignette("data-structures", package = "peridial")`: what the `pd_unit`,
  `pd_patient`, `pd_catheter` and `pd_infection` classes hold, how they fit
  together, and how their constructors keep them consistent.
- `vignette("indicators-classification", package = "peridial")`: how the
  peritonitis rate and the peritonitis-free percentage are calculated, and how
  episodes are classified into relapsing, recurrent and repeat peritonitis.


## Installation and setup

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ernestcaballero/peRidial")
```

> **Note:** peridial includes compiled C++ code (via Rcpp), so installing from
> source requires a working compiler toolchain: Rtools on Windows, or the Xcode
> Command Line Tools on macOS (`xcode-select --install`). Linux users
> typically have a compiler available already.

The package is installed from the `peRidial` repository but loaded under its all-lowercase name:

```{r}
library(peridial)
```


## The example data

The example uses two synthetic Excel files that ship with the package, covering the 2025 reporting year for a fictional unit:

- `a3_2025.xlsx` is the unit survey called `Form A3` file. Each row is one PD catheter. `Patient ID` identifies the patient and it repeats when a patient has more than one catheter in the period. This input also includes the patient's demographic details, PD start and stop dates, dialysis modality, and any change of dialysis modality like transplant, permanent transfer to haemodialysis (HD) or stopped PD. The example file has 62 catheters across 60 patients: 58 patients with a single catheter, and two whose catheter was removed and replaced during the reporting year.
- `pe_2025.xlsx` is the peritonitis episode `Form PE` file. Each row is one peritonitis episode: the date of infection, the organism(s) cultured, the date of the last antibiotic dose, and whether the episode led to hospitalisation, catheter removal or a permanent transfer to HD. The example file has 28 episodes across 17 patients.

No real patient data is included. The synthetic dataset was modelled on published
field definitions: patient- and episode-level data items from the Australia and New
Zealand Dialysis and Transplant Registry (ANZDATA) Data Dictionary and its survey
`Form A3`, and other catheter-level fields such as procedure type and removal
reason from the New Zealand Peritoneal Dialysis Registry (NZPDR), which records them
where `Form A3` does not. The column names are the package author's own, chosen to achieve
the aims of this package, so they match neither an ANZDATA nor an NZPDR export. Values are decoded
rather than coded: `Gender` holds `"Female"`, not a registry code. To prepare your own
data, see *Using your own data* below.


## Building a `pd_unit`

### Building from the example files

`pd_unit()` reads the two files and builds the whole object in one call. Choose a reporting period with a start date `t0` and an end date `t1`, usually the first and last day of a calendar year. Dates are given in `YYYY-MM-DD` format.

```{r}
t0 <- as.Date("2025-01-01")           # first calendar day
t1 <- as.Date("2025-12-31")           # last calenday day

unit <- pd_unit(
  unit_data = system.file("extdata", "a3_2025.xlsx", package = "peridial"),
  infection_data = system.file("extdata", "pe_2025.xlsx", package = "peridial"),
  t0 = t0, t1 = t1, unit_id = "Wellington PD Unit"
)

unit
```

Building this example raises one warning, shown above. It flags SPD0012, who was already on PD at `t0` and whose first episode in the example file is on 2025-01-18, 17 days after `t0`, with no earlier episode in the file. The example file starts at `t0`, so the warning is expected here as an example (see *Include earlier episodes* below). The other two vignettes build the same unit with the warning muted.

`pd_unit()` takes three further arguments, all with defaults. `rate_benchmark` (0.40 episodes per patient-year) and `pf_benchmark` (0.80) are the ISPD targets the unit is judged against. They are carried on the unit and used by `summary()` and `plot()` methods. `censor_on_last_stop` (`TRUE`) treats a patient whose every catheter has closed, with none reopened, as having left PD on the last stop date, which ends their time at risk there. Set it to `FALSE` if your unit records genuine breaks from PD, because a break and a permanent exit look identical in the raw data.

Gaps in the source data found while building (eg. an episode that cannot be matched to an active catheter, an organism that is not on the accepted list, or a permanent transfer to haemodialysis recorded without a reason) are collected and raised together as a single error, and **no** unit is built. Correct them in the source files/data and run `pd_unit()` again until it builds.

Not every problem stops the build. If it can safely carry on with an assumption, it does, and reports the assumption as an R warning instead. The cases are a transplant or a permanent move to haemodialysis that is recorded without a date, more than one column in the file that could be the same expected column, a date that can’t be read (set to missing), and a patient's first episode falling close to `t0` with no earlier episode in the file (see *Using your own data*). For a missing transplant or transfer date, the warning says what the build did in its place: the patient is treated as still on PD, or, if another event or a closed catheter already ended their PD, censored on that date. These warnings are shown only after the error check passes, so a build that fails reports its errors first and the warnings appear once it succeeds; the exception is an unreadable date, which is reported as soon as the file is read. As with errors, check each warning and correct your source files if the assumption is wrong.

### Using your own data

> **Important:** the column names in the synthetic dataset were chosen by the
> package author, so an ANZDATA or NZPDR export will not match them exactly.
> Some differing names are recognised automatically (see below), but a raw
> export will usually need renaming before it loads.

To use your own data:

1. Load it into R, for example with `readr::read_csv()` or
   `readxl::read_excel()`.
2. Select the columns whose meaning most closely matches the columns in the
   table below.
3. Rename them to match, and recode values where needed (for example, coded
   values to plain ones such as `"Female"`).
4. Pass the cleaned tables to `pd_unit()`. `unit_data` and
   `infection_data` each accept a data frame already in R, or the path
   to an `.xlsx` or `.csv` file, so cleaned data held in R does not need to
   be written out first.

Your files must use the column names in the table below. Capitalisation, spacing and punctuation are ignored, so `Patient ID`, `patient_id` and `PatientID` are all read as the same column. Beyond that, `pd_unit()` matches on keywords, so a name that differs but still carries the expected words is picked up. For example,`Infection Date` is read as `Date of Infection`, `DOB` as `Date of Birth`, and `Sex` as `Gender`. A column already named exactly as the target is always kept and where no such column exists and two or more columns could both match one target, the leftmost one in the file is used. The build carries on and a warning names the candidate columns and the name that is chosen.

| File | Required columns | Optional columns |
|---|---|---|
| Unit (A3) | Patient ID, Insertion Date, PD Start Date, Date of Birth | Gender, Ethnicity, Primary Kidney Disease, Height, Weight, Cigarette Smoking Status, Diabetes Type, Procedure Type, PD Stop Date, Removal Reason, Dialysis Type, Dialysis Modality Change, Modality Change Reason, Date Modality Change, Date of Death, Cause of Death, Transplant Date |
| Peritonitis (PE) | Patient ID, Date of Infection, Organism, Last Dose Antibiotic | Overnight Hospitalisation, Days Hospitalised, Catheter Removed, Catheter Removed Date, Interim HD, Permanent HD, First Dialysis Date, Last Dialysis Date |

A missing required column stops the build with an error and provide a list of what was found. Check the spelling of optional columns carefully as a missing optional column is filled with `NA` without a warning. An incorrectly named `Date of Death` or `PD Stop Date` column, for example, means patients are not censored and patient-years are overstated.

**Include earlier episodes.** An episode is classified against the same patient's previous episode, and a relapse is not counted. For a patient who was already on PD at `t0`, an episode in the first 4 weeks of the period may be a relapse of one from before `t0`. If the infection file starts at `t0` that earlier episode is missing, so the later one is counted as new and the rate is overstated. Include episodes from at least 28 days before `t0` (for example the previous reporting period's rows) in the infection file. They are used only for classifying and are not counted in the period. When a patient's first episode falls within 28 days of `t0` and the file holds nothing from more than 28 days before `t0`, `pd_unit()` raises a warning listing those patients so you can check. After checking, a genuine no earlier episode means the warning can be ignored.

Values should follow these formats:

- `Patient ID` must be in NHI format: three letters then four digits (`ABC1234`), case-insensitive. A row whose ID is a different shape is reported and the build stops.
- Dates can be Excel date cells, `Date` columns, or text in `YYYY-MM-DD` or day-first format (`31/01/2025`, `31-01-2025`). A date that cannot be read is set to `NA` with a warning.
- A `.csv` file is read as it is: column names are standardised as for Excel files, and blank cells and `NA` are missing values.
- Yes/no columns accept `Yes`/`No`, `Y`/`N`, `TRUE`/`FALSE` or `1`/`0`.
- Several organisms for one episode go in one cell. A comma, semicolon, `&`, `+`, `/`
  or the word "and" all separate them, so `Coag - Neg Staph, Staph Epidermidis` and
  `S. epidermidis; Staph epidermidis` are both read as two organisms.
- A permanent move to haemodialysis is recorded as `Any PD to HD` in Dialysis Modality Change.


#### Example

The outline below walks through steps 1 to 4. Replace the file names, the source column names (such as MRN and DOB), and the Sex recoding with whatever your own exports use. The quoted names on the left ("Patient ID", "Date of Birth", and so on) are the names pd_unit() expects and should stay as they are.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
raw_a3 <- readxl::read_excel("my_unit_export.xlsx")
raw_pe <- readxl::read_excel("my_peritonitis_export.xlsx")

a3 <- data.frame(
  "Patient ID" = raw_a3$MRN,
  "Date of Birth" = raw_a3$DOB,
  "Insertion Date" = raw_a3$CatheterInsertDate,
  "PD Start Date" = raw_a3$PDStart,
  "Gender" = ifelse(raw_a3$Sex == 1, "Male", "Female"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

pe <- data.frame(
  "Patient ID"  = raw_pe$MRN,
  "Date of Infection" = raw_pe$InfectionDate,
  "Organism" = raw_pe$Organism,
  check.names = FALSE
)

unit <- pd_unit(
  unit_data = a3,
  infection_data = pe,
  t0 = as.Date("2025-01-01"),
  t1 = as.Date("2025-12-31"),
  unit_id = "Your PD Unit"
)
```


### When the build fails

The package also ships a deliberately messy copy of each file, closer to what a real
registry export looks like: `a3_2025_messy.xlsx` and `pe_2025_messy.xlsx`. Between them
they carry renamed columns, blank cells in required fields, two malformed patient IDs,
one self-contradictory catheter record, and organism names written eighteen different
ways. Building from them fails, and every problem is reported in one go:

```{r}
tryCatch(
  pd_unit(
    unit_data = system.file("extdata", "a3_2025_messy.xlsx", package = "peridial"),
    infection_data = system.file("extdata", "pe_2025_messy.xlsx", package = "peridial"),
    t0 = t0, t1 = t1, unit_id = "Messy PD Unit"
  ),
  error = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e))
)
```

Three kinds of problem are listed: missing required values, two patient IDs that are not
three letters followed by four digits, and one catheter that gives a removal reason but no
stop date. The last is reported twice, as cause and as consequence — it was SPD0053's only
catheter, so the patient drops out of the counts and patient-years entirely. One bad cell
can remove a patient from the cohort, which is why the build refuses rather than report a
rate that is missing someone.

Row numbers are the rows as the spreadsheet shows them, header included, so `row 40` is
row 40 in Excel. (A data frame has no header row, so there the count starts at its first
record.) Each row stops at its first problem, so expect to re-run `pd_unit()` a few times.

What is *absent* matters too. No column is reported missing, though the A3 heads its
identifier column `NHI` and its stop date `Date Stopped PD`; the keyword matcher found
both. No organism is reported either, despite `e. coli`, `  STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS `, a tab
before `Enterococcus faecium`, abbreviations like `K pneumoniae`, and two cells holding two
organisms: every organism on the fifteen rows that got that far matched the accepted
list. Spelling and spacing are handled; structural problems are not. The column-matching
warnings described above are not shown here either — a failed build stops at its errors, so
they surface only once these errors are fixed.


## Inspecting a unit

Four S3 methods do the work of inspecting at what was built. `print()` is defined for
every class, `summary()` for a unit and a patient, `plot()` for a unit, and `subset()`
for a unit, a patient or a catheter.

| Method | `pd_unit` | `pd_patient` | `pd_catheter` | `pd_infection` |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| `print()` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `summary()` | yes | yes | -- | -- |
| `plot()` | yes | -- | -- | -- |
| `subset()` | yes | yes | yes | -- |

### `print()`

`print()` gives a short, fixed set of fields for one object. Because the same 
method is defined at each level, an object can be printed wherever it sits in 
the hierarchy. The nested objects are reachable through the unit's `patient_list`:

```{r}
pat <- Filter(function(p) p$patient_id == "SPD0059", unit$patient_list)[[1]]
pat
```

This patient's first catheter was removed and replaced during the year, so they have
two, and they left PD before the period ended. Printing the second catheter shows its
own window and why it was removed:

```{r}
pat$catheters[[2]]
```

A `pd_infection` prints its organisms, its episode type and its outcome. An `NA` 
in outcome means resolved peritonitis case, not missing:

```{r}
spd0003 <- Filter(function(p) p$patient_id == "SPD0003", unit$patient_list)[[1]]
spd0003$catheters[[1]]$infections[[2]]
```

### `summary()`

`summary()` on a unit prints the indicator report: the peritonitis rate and the
peritonitis-free percentage, each judged against the benchmark carried on the object 
(`[ MET ]` or `[ NOT MET ]`), then episodes by type, how patients left PD, 
demographics, catheters and organisms.

```{r}
s <- summary(unit)
```

It also returns those components invisibly, so they can be used directly:

```{r}
s$rate
s$rate_met
s$episode_types
s$demographics$dialysis_type
s$catheters$time_to_first_peritonitis_days["mean"]
```

How the two indicators are defined, and which episodes count towards them, is covered
in `vignette("indicators-classification", package = "peridial")`.

`summary()` on a single patient is the same idea one level down: their status, age,
demographics, each catheter's window and outcome, their total time at risk, and their
countable episodes by type.

```{r}
summary(spd0003)
```

### `plot()`

`plot()` draws the unit's indicators. `type = "monthly"` and `type = "quarterly"` bin
the reporting period into calendar months or quarters and plot the rate in each, with
the benchmark as a reference line:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(unit, type = "monthly")
```

`type = "yearly"` instead plots the cumulative, year-to-date rate and peritonitis-free
percentage as two panels, so both indicators can be read against their benchmarks over
the same period:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(unit, type = "yearly")
```

The bins and the rate in each of them come from `peritonitis_rate_by_period()`, described in `vignette("indicators-classification", package = "peridial")`.

`plot()` needs ggplot2, and `type = "yearly"` also needs patchwork; both are suggested
packages rather than hard dependencies. The reference line defaults to the unit's own
`rate_benchmark` and can be overridden for one plot with `benchmark`. With
`type = "yearly"`, four optional cohort panels can be added underneath, each off by
default:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plot(unit, type = "yearly", benchmark = 0.50,
     show_ip = TRUE,            # incident vs prevalent
     show_pkd = TRUE,           # primary kidney disease
     show_modality = TRUE,      # CAPD / APD / hybrid
     show_stop.reason = TRUE)   # why catheters were stopped
```

### `subset()`

`subset()` asks questions about the data by using filters and conditions. 
It joins the unit's `patients`, `catheters` and `infections` tibbles into one flat table, 
one row per episode carrying its catheter's and its patient's columns, and returns the rows that
meet a condition as a plain tibble:

```{r}
subset(unit, episode_type == "recurrent",
       select = c(patient_id, catheter_id, infection_date, organisms, episode_type))
```

`subset` and `select` are written as in base `subset()`: a logical condition on any
column of the flat table, and column names, ranges (`patient_id:gender`) or negation
(`-t0`). `NA` counts as `FALSE`, so a condition on an episode column keeps only the
rows that have an episode.

A patient with no episodes still has a row, with the episode columns `NA`, and a
patient with several catheters or episodes has several rows, so row counts are not
patient counts:

```{r}
nrow(subset(unit))
nrow(subset(unit, !is.na(infection_date)))
dplyr::n_distinct(subset(unit)$patient_id)
```

Using `subset`, the indicators are not recalculated and the unit is not modified: 
the result is a tibble to inspect, not a smaller `pd_unit`. The same method is 
defined for a patient and for a catheter, over whatever sits below them:

```{r}
subset(pat, select = c(catheter_id, pd_start_date, pd_stop_date, removal_reason))
```
